fields.meta_description: Build an incident report form staff file from a phone. Each report reaches the right manager and lands in a database you own.
fields.h1: Build an Incident Report Form That Reaches the Right Manager
fields.hero_description: Create an incident report form that sends each report to the right person by severity and tracks every fix to done.
fields.features_heading: What Happens After Someone Hits Submit
fields.features_subheading: A paper report sits in a tray until a manager reads it. These six pieces put it in front of the right person during the same shift.
fields.feature_1:
Questions that change with the event type

Pick injury, near miss or theft, and the form asks what that event needs. An injury asks for the body part and the first aid given, while a theft asks for the estimated loss.
fields.feature_2:
Photos and a timestamp on every report

Attach photos from the scene before the report goes in, and the form records the time and place with it. Reviewers see the spilled pallet instead of a description of it.
fields.feature_3:
Severity decides who hears first

Set the rules that route each report. A serious injury emails the safety lead at once, a broken shelf goes to facilities, and a minor scrape waits for the weekly review list.
fields.feature_4:
Each fix gets an owner and a due date

Assign each fix to a person with a due date on the same record as the report. Overdue actions show up on the safety dashboard, and closing one asks for a note on what changed.
fields.feature_5:
Signatures from the people involved

Collect a signature from the reporter or a witness on a phone. The signed copy stays attached to the report, and anyone who has not signed yet gets a reminder the next morning.
fields.feature_6:
Your full codebase, exported to GitHub

Export the code to your GitHub repository on paid plans when IT wants incident reports inside an HR system or a safety platform. Host it on your own servers and extend it.

fields.tab_content_1:
Near misses in aisle 12 reach a supervisor in minutes

Halfway through the night shift at Cedar Ridge Distribution, a reversing forklift clips the rack in aisle 12. A picker files the near miss from her phone with two photos. Any near miss involving a forklift goes to Luis, the shift supervisor, in Slack. He adds a fix, a convex mirror at the aisle end, due Friday.
fields.tab_content_2:
A parent signs for every bite before pickup

Bites happen in toddler rooms, and parents expect to hear the same day. At Little Oak Early Learning, a teacher logs a bite on the playground with the first aid given, using initials only. The report goes to the parent's phone, and the parent reads and signs it before pickup. The director sees any report still unsigned.
fields.tab_content_3:
Losses over $200 go to loss prevention

Linden Street Market loses small amounts of stock to theft every week. A shift lead files each report with the items taken and the estimated loss. A report for $240 in razor cartridges goes to Priya, the regional loss prevention lead, with the camera timestamp attached. Anything under $200 rolls into the monthly count.
fields.tab_content_4:
Eastside logs half of all burns this quarter

Four kitchens file reports into one app at Maple Hall Restaurant Group. The operations director sees every report by location and type. This quarter the group logged 18 burns, and 9 came from the Eastside kitchen. The dashboard flags Eastside, and the director books a fryer station review with its head chef.

fields.howto_title: How to Create an Incident Report Form
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to plan an incident report form that reaches the right person during the shift, then build and test it.
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Decide who hears about each report
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write down every kind of event your team should report, such as injuries and near misses. Each type gets its own follow-up questions. This list shapes the whole form and decides which details a reporter is asked for on the day itself.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Ask for facts the reporter saw: the time, the place, who was there, what happened in order, and what first aid or cleanup followed. Leave out fields that invite guesses about fault. Those questions belong in the investigation that comes after the report.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Choose who gets each report and how fast. A forklift near miss might page the shift supervisor at once, while a cracked floor tile can wait for the weekly safety review. Name a backup person for nights and weekends too.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Paste your incident types and routing rules into one prompt. Emergent builds the form and an incidents table, plus a dashboard by location and type. Change a question or a routing rule later by asking for it in plain English.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Make a photo required for property damage and add a witness section with contact details. Add signature fields where someone has to confirm the record. Keep details about an injured person to what the follow-up needs and nothing more.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Attach a corrective action to every report, with one person responsible and a deadline. The safety lead sees open actions on the dashboard, and an owner with an overdue action gets an email reminder each morning until it is marked done.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Report a fake near miss from a phone in the place it would happen, such as the loading dock. Confirm that the alert reaches the right supervisor, that the photo comes through, and that the corrective action appears on the dashboard.

claims_to_source: OSHA requires employers to report a work-related fatality within 8 hours, and an in-patient hospitalization, amputation or loss of an eye within 24 hours

OSHA guidance says incident investigations should focus on root causes, not on finding fault or blame, and encourages investigating near misses

intent.evidence: Top 10 is OSHA, agency and university PDFs plus template sites; the FAQ gives a definition, where to find free forms, a worked example, what a blank form includes, OSHA 301 timing, tracking and customizing, and the how-to stays on facts versus fault.

craft.evidence: QC Q2/Q5/Q7 clean; "Reviewers see the spilled pallet instead of a description of it."

voice.evidence: "A report filed in a binder explains last month. A report that reaches a supervisor during the shift changes what happens on the next one." No hype vocabulary.

truth.evidence: OSHA 301 within 7 calendar days matches 29 CFR 1904.29 (Cornell); the blame and root-cause line matches osha.gov/incident-investigation; Emergent lines map to claims_used; tab 4 3+9+2+4=18, 9/18=50% matches "half of all burns"; $240 over $200, smaller losses to the monthly count.

findings.fix: Limit it to the university forms ("a university's form was written for its own campus") or drop the sentence.
